sūkṣmakriyā
(‘the subtle process)
------------------------------------------
It is the fourth step in the practice of लययोग. (See LAYAYOGA.)
It consists in withdrawing the मिन्द् from the external sense-objects and concentrating on the light between the eyebrows. This is also called jyotirdhyāna.

sūktavāka
(‘speech of adoration’)
------------------------------------------
This word means the deity अग्नि as also the formula repeated by the होतृ in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
It is chanted by the होतृ priest at a particular stage in the sacrifice when the अध्वर्यु priest and then the आग्नीध्र request him.
The contents of this may be stated briefly as follows:
Praise of हेअवेन् and earth; an appeal to अग्नि (the sacrificial fire) for one’s elevation; various attributes of हेअवेन् and earth; acceptance of the sacrificial offerings by various deities; blessings on the sacrificer; prayer for the attainment of the fruits of sacrifice.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.

śukriya
------------------------------------------
Śukriya is one of the four वेदव्रतस्, preparatory disciplines undertaken before the study of the four वेदस्.
It should be observed for 3 days or 12 days or even one year, as directed by the Vedic teacher. After this, the study of the main parts of the Ṛgveda is begun.
Upanayana has to be performed again before beginning this vrata.
See also VEDAVRATAS.

sūkta
(‘well-said’)
------------------------------------------
The सूक्त is a hymn of the Ṛgveda comprising several ṛks (verses). Some of the famous sūktas are: Puruṣasūkta, Viṣṇusūkta, Śrīsūkta, Nāsadīyasūkta, and so on.
See also ṚGVEDA.

Śukranītisāra
------------------------------------------
This is an abridged edition of an earlier, much bigger, work. The subject matter is both political and non-political. It has four adhyāyas or chapters. The last has seven prakaraṇas or subsections.
It may be assigned to the period circa A.

.
The contents may be stated briefly as follows:
The duties and functions of princes, including that of the crown-prince and some dignitaries; general rules of मोरलित्य् to be observed by the king and his associates; characteristics of a king’s friends or allies; on the royal treasure; arts and sciences; some customs and institutions; duties and functions of the king; forts and armed forces; council of ministers; trade and commerce; public finance; jurisprudence; international law.
The non-political subjects dealt with include architecture, sculpture, painting, manners and morals, fine-arts and literature.
There is a voluminous work called Śukranīti in five chapters, which has been printed in A.

Śuka
------------------------------------------
Śuka, the son of the sage व्यास, was an extremely great and respected sage. He is said to have been born of the celestial maiden Ghṛtācī when she had taken the form of a शुक or parrot, from व्यास.
He had his एदुचतिओन् from his ड़थेर् as also from the king जनक.
His self-control was so great that Rambhā, a reputed apsarā (celestial maiden) failed to entice him by her amorous charms.
It was he who learnt the Bhāgavata from his ड़थेर् व्यास and then taught it to the king परीक्षित् during his last days.
There was another शुक (along with Sāraṇa) who was one of the spies of रावण and who had sneaked into the army camp of राम. However, राम ordered that he be shown everything and sent back to रावण!

Śukrācārya
------------------------------------------
Bṛhaspati and शुक्राचार्य (also known as उशनस्) are the two most colourful personalities met with in the पुराणस्. Whereas बृहस्पति was the गुरु (teacher) of the देवस् (gods), शुक्राचार्य was the गुरु of the दानवस् (demons).
He was the son of the sage भृगु and Pulomā. The great sage च्यवन was his elder brother. By pleasing शिव through severe austerities, he had obtained the sañjīvinī-विद्या, the science of reviving the dead. He had three wives: Śataparvā, Ūrjasvatī and Jayantī. Devayāṇī was his daughter born in Ūrjasvatī.
He lost one eye during वामन’s visit to the king बलि.
Śaṇḍa and Amarka were his sons who became the teachers of the demons later.
See also BṚHASPATI.

sūkṣmadhyāna
(‘subtle contemplation’)
------------------------------------------
When the Kuṇdaliṇi is awakened, and joins the jīvātman (the सोउल्), it leaves the body through astral light (through the portals of the eyes) and the योगि is able to see his own subtle body (liṅgaśarīra).
The Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā (6.18-21) describes this process.

Śukra
(‘the bright one’)
------------------------------------------
Śukra is one of the Nine Planets—the planet Venus. He is an auspicious deity very much interested in making people happy. He follows a course alternating in front of and behind सूर्य the Sun. He possesses a big chariot drawn by eight horses.
In the sky he appears as the brightest planet.
See also NAVAGRAHAS.

Śuklayajurveda Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
The Śuklayajurveda Saṁhitā—also known as the Vājasaneya Saṁhitā—attributed to the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य is said to have 15 शाखास् or recensions. They actually bear the names of the disciples to whom याज्ञवल्क्य taught. Some of them are: Kāṇva, Mādhyandina, Jābāla, Baudheya, Śāpeya, Pārāśara, Baijavāpa and so on.
However, only the first two are extant now, the rest being completely lost.
The Kāṇvaśākhā contains 2086 mantras spread over 40 adhyāyas or chapters. The Mādhyandinaśākhā also has 40 chapters, but only 1900—or 1975 according to another version—mantras.
The entire work is in verses without prose portions as in the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
The following is a brief summary of the contents:
Chapter 1 (31 verses)
Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; त्याग-vrata (resolve to give the object of offering); bringing water and purifying it; spreading the deer-skin; preparing cooked rice; driving away the demons and evil spirits.
Chapter 2 (34 verses)
Purifying the समिध् (faggots) and कुश grass; lighting the fire; keeping the implements in their respective places; prayer for the protection of the sacrifice; putting the samidhs into the fire; keep away a part of the offering for the demons; mantras for getting offspring.
Chapter 3 (63 verses)
Agnyādhāna (producing the fire); अग्निहोत्र; eulogy of the cow; the सावित्रीमन्त्र; worship of the other fires like the आहवनीय; the दीक्षा (taking the vows) of the sacrificer; worship of रुद्र, the three-eyed God.
Chapter 4 (37 verses)
Somayāga and some of its details.
Chapter 5 (43 verses)
Details of the preparation for the सोमयाग are continued here. They include preparation of सोम juice and placing of the appropriate vessels.
Chapter 6 (37 verses)
Erecting the yūpastambha (sacrificial post of wood); tying the animal to it; बलि (immolation and sacrifice); mantras for sending it to हेअवेन्.
Chapter 7 (48 verses)
Filling the सोम juice in various cups meant for the various deities like इन्द्र, वायु, मित्र, वरुण and others.
Chapter 8 (63 verses)
Continuation of the previous topics; some सोम sacrifices like षोडशिन्, Dvādaśin and गवामयन.
Chapter 9 (40 verses)
Vājapeya and राजसूय, two well-known and popular sacrifices of those days, are described here.
Chapter 10 (34 verses)
Description of the Rājasūyayāga is continued here.
Chapter 11 (83 verses)
A detailed description of अग्निचयन (the rite of piling the fire-altar for सोम sacrifices in 5 layers with bricks) is started from this chapter right up to he 18th chapter.
Chapter 12 (117 verses)
Viṣṇukrama (taking 4 steps with appropriate mantras), Vaṇīvāhana rite (coming and going of fire kept in a vessel on a cart), purification of the place, bringing the bricks and so on—these are the topics of this chapter.
Chapters 13 to 15 (153 verses)
They describe in detail the building up the altar with 10,008 bricks in four layers, in the form of a bird with its wings stretched.
Chapter 16 (66 verses)
The entire chapter contains the famous Rudrādhyāya. It is used in the Śatarudrīya होम. (It appears in the Taittirīya Saṁhitā [4.5] also.)
Chapter 17 (99 verses)
Ascending the वेदि (the altar), inviting the Fire-god, offering मधुपर्क (See MADHUPARKA.), praising अग्नि and इन्द्र, pouring of milk and a few more rites are described here.
Chapter 18 (77 verses)
This contains the mantras used in वसोर्धारा (‘flow of wealth’), an oblation of ghee poured in a continuous stream into the fire on the altar.
Chapter 19 (95 verses)
The topics dealt with are: the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice; offering milk to the deities—the अश्विन्स्, इन्द्र and सरस्वती; offering wine, after purifying with mantras, into the दक्षिणाग्नि; praising the पितृस् (manes) like the Agniṣvāttas; story of इन्द्र being rejuvenated by the अश्विन्स्.
Chapter 20 (90 verses)
The subjects of this chapter are: मन्त्र for one’s welfare: अवभृथ (final bath) of the sacrificer; मन्त्र for destruction of sins; giving sacrificial ड़ोओद् to इन्द्र; chanting of the Āprīsūktas (See ĀPRĪ.); inviting इन्द्र; hymns to the अश्विन्स्, सरस्वती and अग्नि.
Chapter 21 (60 verses)
This contains the following topics: hymns to वरुण and अग्नि; worship of अदिति the मोथेर् of gods; oblations to Mitrā-वरुण; chanting of Indrasūkta; conclusion of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice.
Chapter 22 (34 verses)
The topic of the अश्वमेध sacrifice is begun here and continues with the details through Chapters 23 (65 verses), 24 (40 verses) and 25 (47 verses).
Chapters 26 (26 verses); 27 (45 verses); 28 (46 verses) and 29 (60 verses)
Various minor sacrifices, conclusion of अश्वमेध sacrifice, hymn to the horse and the Sun-god identifying the two as one, eulogy of the weapons of war—these are the topics described here.
Chapters 30 (22 verses) and 31 (22 verses)
The sacrifice called पुरुषमेध (human sacrifice) is described here with 184 varieties of living beings as the offering! Scholars however describe it as only symbolical.
Chapters 32 (16 verses) and 33 (97 verses)
These deal with the sacrifice called Sarvamedha. Along with the praise of the sacrificer there is a prayer for granting knowledge, wisdom and wealth. There are several mantras and yajus (prose passages) in praise of several deities.
Chapter 34 (58 verses)
The first six mantras are known as the Śivasaṅkalpopaniṣad. This is followed by some details of a few sacrifices and hymns of praise of the deities भग, पूषन् and ब्रह्मणस्पति.
Chapter 35 (22 verses)
Pitṛmedha mantras are the chief content here.
(See PITṚMEDHA for details.)
Chapters 36 to 39 (86 verses)
These contain the mantras connected with the प्रवर्ग्य rite. (See PRAVARGYA.)
Chapter 40 (18 verses)
This is the famous Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad
Some important aspects of the teaching of the Saṁhitā are:
Meticulous performance of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् was considered the highest puruṣārtha. Even the gods got special powers by performing sacrifices. Mantras are very powerful, if chanted correctly and will harm if chanted wrongly, the power being dependent on the correctness of chanting.
See ĪŚĀVĀSYA UPANIṢAD.
